items.title: Issue Intent — End-to-End GitHub Issue Classification
items.brief: Built an end-to-end GitHub issue classifier achieving 88.66% Micro F1 with PyTorch DistilBERT on 142,320 held-out issues, with separately evaluated ONNX INT8 browser deployment.

details.overview: An end-to-end NLP and ML engineering project that classifies GitHub issues into bug, feature, question, and documentation. Covers dataset quality auditing, reproducible experiments, transformer fine-tuning, model optimization, and deployment through both a browser-based application and a containerized inference API.
details.problem: GitHub repositories receive large volumes of issues covering different intents. Manually categorizing these reports takes time and can delay issue triage. This project explores automated intent classification to help organize incoming issues and support maintainers.
objectives: Build a reproducible classification pipeline using real GitHub issue reports.
Compare classical NLP, neural networks, and transformer-based approaches.
Evaluate the selected model on the official held-out benchmark.
Optimize model size and CPU inference using ONNX INT8 quantization.
Deploy an interactive browser application without requiring a continuously running inference server.
details.dataset: NLBSE 2023 Issue Report Classification — 1,418,201 real GitHub issues, including 1,275,881 original training records and 142,320 official test examples. After exact-text deduplication and conflicting-label filtering, 1,221,982 records remained for training and validation.
details.methodology: Dataset audit and cleaning → Stratified train/validation split → TF-IDF classical baselines → Structured text preprocessing → PyTorch TextCNN → DistilBERT fine-tuning → Official test evaluation → ONNX FP32 export and INT8 quantization → React browser inference and Cloudflare Pages deployment.
kpis: 88.66% Micro F1 and 79.12% Macro F1 on the 142,320-example official test set (PyTorch DistilBERT).
48.17% reduction in ONNX model size after INT8 quantization.
372 Python tests and 19 frontend tests passed.
Browser-based inference using ONNX Runtime Web and WASM.
insights: DistilBERT achieved stronger validation F1 scores than the reported classical and TextCNN baselines.
Selecting the checkpoint by validation Macro F1 helped account for performance on less frequent issue classes.
INT8 quantization reduced the ONNX graph from 255.54 MiB to 132.44 MiB.
Hosting model weights on Hugging Face enabled a static Cloudflare Pages application with inference executed locally in the browser.
challenges: Handling duplicate reports, conflicting labels, and class imbalance in a large real-world text dataset.
Designing structured preprocessing and token budgeting for long GitHub issue descriptions.
Training and evaluating transformer models under limited compute resources.
Maintaining preprocessing and tokenizer parity between Python and browser inference.
Optimizing ONNX model loading and deployment for static hosting.

items.title: ADAS Graduation Project
items.brief: Developed computer vision components for an ADAS prototype integrating driver recognition, drowsiness monitoring, YOLOv8 traffic sign detection, and Raspberry Pi edge inference alongside V2V communication.

details.overview: A team-developed AI, IoT, and embedded systems ADAS prototype combining driver authentication, landmark-based driver monitoring, YOLOv8 traffic sign recognition on Raspberry Pi, V2V communication, and a Firebase-connected dashboard.
details.problem: Road accidents are often caused by driver fatigue, distraction, unauthorized vehicle access, missed traffic signs, and the lack of communication between nearby vehicles. The project addresses these challenges by combining Computer Vision, Edge AI, and V2V technologies into a unified safety system.
objectives: Authenticate drivers with facial recognition before vehicle operation.
Detect drowsiness and distraction using facial landmarks and Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR).
Recognize traffic signs using YOLOv8 on Raspberry Pi.
Exchange vehicle warnings over ESP-NOW with AES encryption.
Connect AI modules to embedded hardware using sockets and SPI.
Display vehicle status and alerts through Firebase and a graphical dashboard.
details.dataset: Traffic Sign Recognition was trained using the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB) dataset. Driver Face Recognition relies on registered user images, while Driver Monitoring operates using real-time facial landmarks without requiring model training.
details.methodology: Driver authentication with face_recognition → dlib facial landmarks and EAR-based monitoring → YOLOv8 traffic sign detection on Raspberry Pi → Socket communication between laptop and Raspberry Pi → SPI integration with embedded controllers → ESP-NOW/AES V2V messaging → Firebase status visualization.
kpis: Driver authentication and drowsiness-monitoring prototype capabilities.
YOLOv8-based traffic sign detection on Raspberry Pi.
Socket and SPI communication between AI and embedded modules.
ESP-NOW V2V warning messages with AES encryption.
insights: Facial recognition, landmark-based monitoring, and YOLOv8 address different driver and road-safety functions.
Running traffic sign inference on Raspberry Pi demonstrates edge deployment within a multi-device prototype.
Socket, SPI, and ESP-NOW links connect computer vision outputs to embedded and V2V components.
Firebase provides a shared status layer for the graphical dashboard.
challenges: Deploying computer vision workloads efficiently across heterogeneous hardware.
Maintaining real-time performance while running multiple AI modules simultaneously.
Synchronizing communication between Laptop, Raspberry Pi, ESP32, and Firebase.
Balancing inference speed and accuracy for edge deployment.

Exported a fitted preprocessing-and-model pipeline for use in a Streamlit application

Selecting the most predictive features

items.title: NEAT Self-Driving Car Simulation
items.brief: Built a Pygame NEAT driving simulation with 30 evolving cars per generation, five distance sensors, four actions, and a 10-generation run.

details.overview: A neural network evolution simulation where cars learn autonomous driving through the NEAT genetic algorithm.
details.problem: Demonstrating how evolutionary algorithms can solve complex autonomous driving behavior without pre-labeled training data.
objectives: Implement NEAT evolutionary algorithm
Train autonomous driving behavior
Visualize evolution across generations
details.dataset: Sensor-based fitness scoring from simulated environment
details.methodology: Pygame driving simulation → NEAT population of 30 agents → Five distance-sensor inputs per car → Four neural-network driving actions → Distance-based fitness updates → Evolution over up to 10 generations
kpis: 5 distance sensors per car and 4 driving actions
insights: NEAT evolves both network connections and weights using fitness feedback from the simulation
Each car uses five distance measurements to select among four driving actions
Distance traveled contributes to the fitness assigned to each evolving agent
challenges: Designing a meaningful fitness function
Balancing exploration vs exploitation in NEAT
